text.p: These are leading stories in this morning's Paris newspapers.
LES ECHOS
-- New car registrations fell by 34 percent in June from June of 1996.
-- Prime Minister Lionel Jospin under pressure from his Socialist party to re-establish an administrative approval for job layoffs.
-- Total oil group chairman Thierry Desmarest says in an interview the group is aiming for a 12 percent return on equity by 2000.

-- Euris to bring its stake in Moulinex appliance manufacturers down to seven percent of capital, Moulinex is implementing a capital restructuring to absorb its controlling holdings Financiere Moulinex and Finap.
-- Generale des Eaux sells its health-sector subsidiary Generale de Sante to Britain's Cinven for 8.6 billion francs.
LA TRIBUNE
-- Government considers raising taxes on companies' profits in 1997.
-- French and British authorities may extend Eurotunnel SA/Plc concession by at least 34 years provided shareholders approve the financial restructuring.
-- Blue-chip CAC-40 index nears 3,000 points, closed at a historical record high on Tuesday at 2,944.04.
-- Swiss insurer Zurich Assurances may be interested in GAN.
LE FIGARO-ECONOMIE
-- Employment and Solidarity Minister Martine Aubry confirms a conference on employment is to be held in mid-September.

-- Renault chairman Louis Schweitzer and PSA chairman Jacques Calvet call on the government to reconsider its position on schemes aiming to rejuvenate workforces, do not favour further government incentive measures for buyers of new cars.

-- Giat Industries chairman Jacques Loppion estimates the company needs around four billion francs a year in recapitalisation over the next three years, adds orders are fifty percent lower than expected.
LIBERATION (Economic section)

-- Some 10 billion francs to be made available to the government by mid-July to finance first wave of measures including a rise in the "back to school" allowance, a rise in housing benefits, a rise in the minimum wage, and the launch of youth employment measures.
THE INTERNATIONAL HERALD TRIBUNE
-- Air France pilot union turns to a U.S. pilots' union to assess cost cuts called for by the airline's management.
